title: Man Arrested Near White House with Guns, Claims He Planned to Kill Trump, DHS Says
body:
A man armed with multiple firearms was taken into custody on Thursday night just blocks from the White House after telling Secret Service agents that he intended to assassinate President Donald Trump. The suspect, an undocumented immigrant, allegedly claimed that voices in his head directed him to travel to Washington, D.C., and carry out the plot. Officers discovered three weapons inside his vehicle and arrested him without incident, according to officials from the Department of Homeland Security.

The incident unfolded shortly after midnight near Lafayette Square, an area that has long been a focal point for protests and security operations. Secret Service personnel, who were conducting routine patrols, observed the suspect’s vehicle parked in a restricted zone and approached to verify its occupants. During the encounter, the man reportedly confessed his intentions and cited auditory hallucinations as the source of his motivation. Agents immediately secured the weapons—a handgun, a rifle and a shotgun—and escorted the suspect to a federal detention facility.

Law enforcement officials emphasized that the suspect’s immigration status was a factor in the investigation, but they stressed that the primary concern was the immediate threat to the president and public safety. “We act on any credible threat, regardless of the individual’s background,” a senior DHS spokesperson said. The Department of Justice has opened a federal case, and the suspect faces charges that could include attempted murder of a federal official, unlawful possession of firearms, and violations of immigration law.

While the arrest prevented a potential attack, it also reignited debate over security protocols surrounding the White House and the broader issue of political violence in the United States. Critics have argued that the Secret Service’s presence in the area has been insufficiently visible, allowing individuals to approach within a short distance of the executive mansion. In response, the agency announced a review of its patrol patterns and will increase the number of agents stationed near high‑profile government sites during periods of heightened tension.

The case also underscores growing concerns about mental health and extremist ideation intersecting with access to weapons. Mental health professionals note that auditory hallucinations, while a symptom of certain disorders, do not inherently predict violent behavior; however, when combined with extremist rhetoric, they can become a dangerous catalyst. Federal authorities have indicated that a comprehensive psychological evaluation will be part of the suspect’s pre‑trial process, aiming to determine the extent to which his mental state influenced his actions.

As the nation watches the legal proceedings unfold, the incident serves as a reminder of the persistent threats faced by elected officials and the importance of vigilant security measures. The Department of Homeland Security has pledged to collaborate with local law‑enforcement agencies to enhance intelligence sharing and to monitor individuals exhibiting signs of radicalization. With the investigation ongoing, officials anticipate that additional details about the suspect’s background and any potential accomplices will emerge, shaping future policies aimed at preventing similar plots from materializing.
